title: Gloria Steinem: An icon of American feminism
description: How Gloria Steinem changed the lives of generations of womenImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Gloria Steinem pictured in 1990 in her New York C
body: How Gloria Steinem changed the lives of generations of womenImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Gloria Steinem pictured in 1990 in her New York City apartmentByTiffany WertheimerUpdated 4 hours agoGloria Steinem was a powerful icon of America's feminist movement and her career spanned numerous roles that changed the lives of generations of women.With her iconic aviator sunglasses and long, blonde-streaked hair - which she considered rebellious in the 1970s - Steinem was an internationally recognised activist in the fight for women's equality.She spoke out for the legalisation of abortion, same-sex marriage, and equal rights and pay for women, and protested against the death penalty and female genital mutilation.Her activism was not without a backlash - from both men and women - and harassment that could be as vulgar as it was intimidating.The early yearsBorn on 25 March 1934 in Toledo, Ohio, Gloria Steinem did not have an easy childhood.Her father Leo Steinem was a travelling salesman and, together with her mother Ruth and older sister Susanne, they lived in a caravan, crisscrossing the country.Leo abandoned the family and moved to California when Steinem was 10 years old, leaving her to care for Ruth who had long suffered with mental illness and had terrifying hallucinations. As a result, Steinem did not go to school full-time until she was 12 years old.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Gloria Steinem at the 1972 Democratic ConventionShe would later remark that she had never wanted children because she had already had one - her mother.In the late 1950s she went to India on a research scholarship, and spent two years in a variety of roles, including helping village women organise non-violent protests against government policies, which sparked her interest in grassroots activism.Steinem left India and moved to New York City in the early 1960s to start her career as a freelance writer. It was a time when male-dominated newsrooms made it difficult for women to get hard-hitting stories.Breakthrough articleHer big break came in 1963, when Steinem went undercover as a Playboy Bunny cocktail waitress and wrote A Bunny's Tale, an exposé for Show magazine detailing the seedy and sexist reality of Hugh Hefner's empire.As soon as she arrived for the interview, a security guard called out, "Here bunny, bunny, bunny."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Steinem's undercover work as a Playboy Bunny revealed a world of misogyny and exploitationUsing the fake name Marie, she lied about her age - telling Playboy she was 24 years old when she was actually four years older.Steinem lifted the lid on the underpaid life of a Bunny, and the physical pain of wearing the high-heels and tight corsets for hours.Despite the fame - and infamy - that followed, she still found herself struggling to be taken seriously by editors. Though the Playboy exposé helped land her assignments for the New York Times and New York Magazine, often they were about ladies' stockings and the latest hairstyles."To this day when people don't like me they introduce me as a former Bunny, as a put-down," she told the New York Times in 2016. "On the other hand, I did improve the working conditions for those women."All-female journalismUndaunted, by 1968 Steinem was a columnist for New York Magazine, focusing on progressive social issues and women's rights.Her article, After Black Power, Women's Liberation, external brought her national fame, making her the face of the US feminist movement in the 1970s."I was the only woman, and after I wrote an abortion article, my [male] friends there said to me: 'Don't get involved with these crazy women. You've worked hard to be taken seriously,'" she told Rachel Cooke for The Guardian in 2011.So she took matters into her own hands.In 1972, she launched Ms. magazine with a group of feminist activists. It was the first all-female founded and operated periodical, designed to be an alternative to other women's magazines that typically focused on housekeeping and fashion.Image source, EPAImage caption, Ms. magazine broke new ground, selling out within its first week of publicationCritics - mainly men - were quick to write it off. News presenter Harry Reasoner said he gave it six months "before they run out of things to say".The first issue sold out within a week and generated 26,000 subscribers. The magazine is still going today.In 1978, Steinem wrote one of Ms. magazine's most infamous and widely read essays - If Men Could Menstruate. Her satirical reflection on how different power, political and economic structures might be if men had menstrual cycles is still referred to in discussions about gender roles.By the end of her career, Steinem had become a prolific and award-winning writer, penning numerous books including her own memoirs, a biography on Marilyn Monroe and a collection of her own famous quotes in the wryly titled, ‪The Truth Will Set You Free, But First It Will Piss You Off.Abortion rights campaignerThough still considered one of the world's best-known feminist activists, Steinem came to advocacy rather late in life - in her thirties.At an abortion awareness rally in 1969 where women were sharing their experiences of having abortions, Steinem was encouraged to share her own story about terminating a pregnancy. It had taken place years earlier in London when she was 22 years old, just before going to India.Abortion was illegal in the UK at the time, unless the woman's mental or physical health was in danger. The doctor took a great risk for Steinem, telling her: "You must promise me two things. First, you will not tell anyone my name. Second, you will do what you want to do with your life."Nearly 60 years later, Steinem broke one of those promises, when she dedicated her memoir, My Life On The Road, to Dr John Sharpe.She described that abortion speak-out event as a "light bulb moment" - when she realised the US needed a bigger women's rights movement.Almost overnight, Steinem became a crusader for abortion rights, calling it "reproductive freedom". The phrase she coined is credited with making the subject more approachable for political discussion and continues to be used in abortion debates.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Joining Steinem at the 1989 March for Women’s Lives were Susan Sarandon, Gloria Allred, Jesse Jackson and Jane FondaSteinem organised marches and quickly became a draw at demonstrations, although she admitted later that she found talking to the huge crowds "utterly terrifying".After Congress failed to pass the Equal Rights Amendment (ERA) in 1970 - legislation granting women equal rights to men - Steinem co-founded the National Women's Political Caucus with fellow feminist leaders and more than 300 women across the US. The group worked to include women in all aspects of political and public life.The same year, she testified at Senate hearings for the ERA, telling the predominantly male audience: "I have been refused service in public restaurants, ordered out of public gathering places and turned away from apartment rentals all for the clearly stated, sole reason that I am a woman."Second-wave feminism continued to gain momentum and Steinem was one of its most famous figureheads.She was also supportive of same-sex marriage, but was criticised for an essay she wrote in 1977 on transgender people. She clarified her position in 2013, saying the words in her "old essay" had been taken "out of time and context"."I believe that transgender people, including those who have transitioned, are living out real, authentic lives. Those lives should be celebrated, not questioned," she wrote in an opinion piece, external.Steinem was also criticised for a 1998 essay in the New York Times, where she showed support for then-President Bill Clinton after news broke of his scandalous affair with intern Monica Lewinsky - who was 22 years old at the time."The truth is that even if the allegations are true, the president is not guilty of sexual harassment," Steinem wrote. "He is accused of having made a gross, dumb and reckless pass at a supporter during a low point in her life."In 2017, she said she "wouldn't write the same thing now".Too glamorous?Critics came from the left as well as right, targeting Steinem for everything from her looks to her motives. Some claimed she was too glamorous to be a true feminist, while others said she was successful only because of her appearance.Betty Friedan, author of The Feminine Mystique, the book credited with launching second-wave feminism, was annoyed that Steinem became the face of the movement, accusing her of "ripping off the movement for private profit" when she launched Ms.The media were trying "to make her a celebrity," fumed Friedan, "but no one should mistake her for a leader."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Steinem's sudden rise to become the face of second-wave feminism caught the ire of some activistsUS President Richard Nixon was recorded during a secret conversation furiously ranting about Steinem, to which she responded: "There is some opinion that Richard Nixon is the most sexually insecure chief of state since Napoleon".Al Goldstein, the notorious pornographer and publisher of Screw magazine, launched a campaign of attacks that included publishing her phone number next to fake advertisements for oral sex.He also printed a graphic centrefold image of a Steinem look-alike, and hung it open on display at the newsstand outside Ms. magazine's office building. She had to look at it every day.As she got older, harassment to this degree became less common. However, given she was a recognisable figure in New York City, it was not uncommon for Steinem to be stopped on the street by strangers wanting to debate - sometimes with an edge of hostility.But she welcomed the continued debate. In 2020, she was among a cross-section of public figures who signed an open letter denouncing cancel culture, saying it weakens open debate by shutting people down."If you care about having the conversation, surely you want to try in a humane way to convince the other person, not do away with them," she told the New York Times.'I can't mate in captivity'Gloria Steinem once quipped: "I can't mate in captivity" - a reference to her disinterest in marriage. But she publicly enjoyed a healthy dating life with a number of rich and famous bachelors, giving critics more ammunition to use against her.They included Frank Thomas who was head of the Ford Foundation; film director Mike Nichols and Olympic decathlete Rafer Johnson (who helped tackle the man who assassinated Robert F Kennedy in 1968)."I was the one always accused of using men, of being too sexual. Someone once sent me a cartoon of a tombstone that said 'at last she sleeps alone'," she wrote.But in 2000, aged 66, she wed David Bale, a South African-born entrepreneur-environmentalist, and father of actor Christian Bale.At the time, the union drew gasps of surprise and even disappointment from some feminists, who had spent years following Steinem's heated debates surrounding marriage laws.But she said those laws had finally changed. "If I had married when I was supposed to get married, I would have lost my name, my legal residence, my credit rating, many of my civil rights. That's not true anymore. It's possible to make an equal marriage," she explained years later.Steinem also confessed to it being a "green card marriage" because Bale's US visa was running out - but said that they loved each other and were going to be together regardless.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, David Bale and Gloria Steinem, pictured with Maurine RothschildBale died three years later from brain lymphoma.Steinem had her own health scare with breast cancer in 1986, and underwent a lumpectomy.'So much to do'Gloria Steinem once said she wanted to live to 100 because "there's so much to do".In her near-century of life, she even became a talented tap dancer.She was given America's highest civilian honour - the Presidential Medal of Freedom - in 2013 by President Barack Obama, who credited her work with giving more women "the respect and opportunities that they deserve".In 2024, she reached the age of 90. She lived alone in New York, content in the knowledge that Ms. Magazine was still publishing.Steinem seized the occasion to tell the BBC that she hoped her legacy "might help individual people... to become more the unique, valuable, loved and lovable person that they want to be."She will be remembered for amplifying the voices of women in a way that mainstream media at the time either could not, or would not.And, in so doing, she altered the landscape and language of women's rights in America.

schema.headline: Gloria Steinem: An icon of American feminism

title: Gloria Steinem: Feminist activist and journalist dies, aged 92
description: Gloria Steinem, who became a leader of the women's liberation movement in the US, has died aged 92. In a post on Instagram, her foundation said she "p
body: Gloria Steinem, who became a leader of the women's liberation movement in the US, has died aged 92. In a post on Instagram, her foundation said she "passed away peacefully" at her home in New York City on Wednesday, "surrounded by many who loved her". Steinem, who was a writer and magazine editor, co-founded the Women's Action Alliance - a group dedicated to fighting sexism - more than 50 years ago.She started her career as a journalist in New York and went on to co-found Ms. magazine, one of the first publications to focus on women's issues other than housekeeping and beauty.During the 1970s, Steinem was a vocal campaigner for women's reproductive rights, among other causes.She herself obtained an illegal abortion in London when she was 22 years old, and years later celebrated the US Supreme Court's 1973 ruling in the case of Roe v Wade, which granted women the constitutional right to abortion. Nearly half a century later she witnessed the reversal of this decision.She also spoke out in favour of the legalisation of same-sex marriage, as well as equal rights and pay for women, and protested against the death penalty and female genital mutilation.Born on 25 March 1934 in Toledo, Ohio, she had a difficult childhood and did not go to school full-time until she was 12 years old.After university in the late 1950s, she went to India on a research scholarship and spent two years in a variety of roles, including helping village women organise non-violent protests against government policies, which sparked her interest in grassroots activism.She then moved to New York City in the early 1960s to start her career as a freelance writer. Her big break came through an exposé of Playboy Bunny working conditions. Eventually she became a columnist for New York Magazine, before founding Ms. magazine in 1972. Famously eschewing marriage, she went on to tie the knot in 2000 to David Bale, a South African-born entrepreneur-environmentalist and father of actor Christian Bale. He died three years later from brain lymphoma.In 2013, then-President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest civilian honour in the US.Her foundation said "she continued working for equality until the very end"."Gloria's greatest gift was her ability to listen to others, to make others feel seen and heard. Her words, actions and example gave people permission to be their truest selves. Gloria lived true to her independent spirit, always with curiosity and a great sense of humour."Her foundation said she lived her last years being in community and writing - welcoming guests into her home for "Talking Circles" - a tradition that will continue.Her commitment to her home becoming a centre for social justice movements, and a forthcoming book An Unexpected Life, are "among many gifts Gloria has given the world with the hope they have ripple effects for generations to come", the foundation said.Tributes flowed on Thursday after the news of her death, with writers and feminists commenting on Instagram with gratitude, some of them saying she had changed their lives.Meghan Markle "celebrated the life and legacy of my friend and mentor", along with pictures of the pair on Instagram."You all know her many accolades and the way in which she helped shape the world for woman and all people", Markle said, but added that beyond their work together, Steinem "privately, was even better than you would imagine".Steinem spent Thanksgiving with Markle's family, introduced the younger woman to one of her best friends, loved "our children with her whole heart, counseling me during hard times, and giving extraordinary advice and perspective with a cup of tea and an unrivaled cheekiness and wit", she said.Markle now wears "with pride" a bracelet Steinem gave her that says "we are linked, not ranked".Former US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton and 2016 presidential candidate said Steinem was "one of the architects of the entire structure of women's equality, I mean tearing down those obstacles to young women being able to participate where their talents and hard work took them"."Gloria was at heart an optimist," Clinton told CBS Mornings on Thursday. "Her activism was rooted in optimism, and that's a moral choice, and she made it every day."

schema.headline: Gloria Steinem: Feminist activist and journalist dies, aged 92

title: Households warned gas price spike could pile fresh pressure on energy bills
description: Households across the UK are being warned to brace for higher energy bills this winter as European countries scramble to replenish their natural gas s
body: Households across the UK are being warned to brace for higher energy bills this winter as European countries scramble to replenish their natural gas stores before the weather dips.Wholesale natural gas prices are already at three-year highs, which could lead to increased energy bills for businesses and consumers.Europe, which delayed its summer stockpiling due to high wholesale costs sparked by the Iran war, had been gambling the conflict would end before winter and prices would in turn fall. Storage levels are significantly lower than usual for this time of year, with countries facing the prospect of rushing to buy gas now or paying potentially higher prices when the winter comes.The European benchmark natural gas price topped €75/MWh on Wednesday, its highest level since late 2022, the tail end of a spike caused by Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Natural gas prices in the UK this week topped 185p per therm, also the highest since late 2022.The price has jumped in the past week amid a return to hostilities between the US and Iran, with analysts fearing the renewed fighting will keep the key Strait of Hormuz closed even longer. Typically, around a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) is transported through the waterway.Hamad Hussain, senior climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, said he did not expect the waterway to begin reopening until early 2027.Even then, there will be a lag before energy is flowing freely through the strait and pressure on energy prices are eased. "The risks to gas prices are definitely tilted towards the upside," Hussain told the BBC, warning that the gas price would top €80 by the end of this year.Hussain recalled interviews with gas storage operators at the outbreak of the US-Israeli war in Iran saying they would wait three to four months for the crisis to ease before stocking up. "We are about six months into the strait being effectively closed and that obviously has not happened," he added.Higher wholesale gas prices feed through to household energy bills by helping determine regulator Ofgem's price cap.The energy price cap rose in July, and will increase by 4% in October, leaving a typical household paying £1,723. But analysts at the energy consultancy Cornwall Insight have forecast domestic energy prices could rise a further 9% in the new year, bringing renewed concern to households during the coldest months.Dr Craig Lowrey, principal consultant at Cornwall Insight, told the BBC on Thursday  a fresh increase in wholesale prices would "increase pressure on our January price cap forecast". However, he cautioned that there was "plenty of time to go" and a fall in wholesale prices could ease the pressure.The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) said gas prices are determined on international markets, dismissing criticism of the UK's own low levels of storage.The boss of British Gas owner Centrica, Chris O'Shea, has repeatedly called for support from the government to expand its Rough storage facility in the North Sea, warning it has been unviable to fill it up and that it will close next year without a deal."We have almost no gas in storage in the UK for the coming winter and this is a huge concern as energy security is national security," he said on LinkedIn, external last week.A DESNZ spokesman said: "We remain open to discussing proposals on all gas storage sites, as long as it provides value for money for taxpayers."The department also pointed to Prime Minister Andy Burnham's pledge to cut VAT from energy bills from October, as well as government action to reduce Britain's reliance on natural gas altogether.Ángel Talavera, chief European economist at Oxford Economics, said there is a "glass half full, and a glass half empty" picture unfolding. On one hand, wholesale gas prices are significantly lower than during the crisis which followed Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.On the other, households and businesses will still face significantly higher energy bills than usual over the coming months. "It's serious, but not catastrophic," he told the BBC, adding "something would have to dramatically change to lower prices".He pointed to a reduction in demand for natural gas in general as a result of the shift towards renewables, but said the overall picture depends hugely on the winter weather."If you have a warmer winter than average, that will be great for demand," he said. But he warned a colder than average winter would have the opposite effect, driving up demand for energy and pushing up prices.It is not known how the developing El Niño over the Pacific Ocean will impact Britain's winter. The so-called Big Freeze of winter 2009-10 was, at the time, the coldest in three decades - and this coincided with an El Niño.However, 2006-07 was also an El Niño winter and that was unseasonably warm.Talavera said gas prices could come down if the weather helps reduce demand and the Strait of Hormuz reopens sooner than expected. But, at the moment, "the weather machine remains our main hope". It comes as a recent spike in the UK government's borrowing costs eased. After a sharp uptick on Tuesday, which took the yield on a 10-year bond - or gilt - to the highest level since 2008, it fell back slightly on Thursday. Yields are hovering around 5.15%, however, which would still represent a post-2008 peak were it not for Tuesday's jump.

schema.headline: Households warned gas price spike could pile fresh pressure on energy bills

title: Anthony Joshua's driver attempted overtake before fatal crash, trial hears
description: Image caption, Adeniyi Mobolaji Kayode, right, leaves court with his lawyer on ThursdayBySimi JolaosoAfrica correspondentReporting fromSagamuThe drive
body: Image caption, Adeniyi Mobolaji Kayode, right, leaves court with his lawyer on ThursdayBySimi JolaosoAfrica correspondentReporting fromSagamuThe driver of a car carrying Anthony Joshua was attempting to overtake another vehicle when it crashed, killing two of the boxer's friends, a court in Nigeria has heard.Adeniyi Mobolaji Kayode, 46, faces charges including causing death by dangerous driving and driving without a valid national driver's licence. He denies the charges.The court was told that the group - who had been travelling to visit Joshua's father in Ogun State, near Lagos in Nigeria, last December - were asleep when Kayode lost control of his Lexus SUV while he overtook a moving truck and collided with a parked lorry.Joshua's personal trainer, Latif Ayodele, and strength coach, Sina Ghami, died in the crash.A second defendant Abubakar Adamu, 35, the driver of the stationary lorry the car collided with, denies a charge against him of obstructing the free flow of traffic.Inspector Christopher Ajayi Taiwo of the Ogun State Motor Traffic Division told the court that by the time he arrived at the scene, both the damaged Lexus and the stationary lorry had been removed.But debris from the crash and soya beans scattered on the road from the lorry's load were found by officers, he added. The only items recovered from the Lexus were a logbook, painkillers and an energy drink, which were found near the driver's side, Ajayi said.Image source, Social MediaImage caption, The former heavyweight champion was a passenger in the crash, which killed his team members Latif Ayodele (left) and Sina Ghami (right)The court heard police has yet to take a statement from Joshua following the crash.During cross-examination, Kayode's lawyer questioned Ajayi over the lack of statement, to which he replied that "efforts are ongoing" and that he had not contacted Joshua because he "didn't have his number".The trial was adjourned until 10 September.Joshua, who was born in Watford, has family roots in Sagamu - a town in Ogun state, near the crash site.After the collision, the boxer posted a tribute to Ghami and Ayodele on social media."I didn't even realise how special they are," he wrote."I'll just be walking with them and cracking jokes with them, not even knowing God kept me in the presence of great men."100% it's tough for me, but I know it's even tougher for their parents."

schema.headline: Anthony Joshua's driver attempted overtake before fatal crash, trial hears

title: Chris Mason: Reform face headwinds as they gather for conference
description: Reform UK begin their annual conference in Birmingham a bigger party than they were a year ago, their numbers swelled at Westminster, at Holyrood, in
body: Reform UK begin their annual conference in Birmingham a bigger party than they were a year ago, their numbers swelled at Westminster, at Holyrood, in the Senedd and in local authorities.But they also gather amid significant political headwinds, much of which revolve around money.There was that whopping £5m gift to Nigel Farage from Christopher Harborne, the Thailand based British billionaire, and the long running row about whether the money should have been declared by Farage once he became an MP.Then there is, among other things, the Metropolitan Police investigation into donations to the party during the last general election campaign.Reform insists that it "takes pride in its stringent vetting of donations."When the party got together in the same West Midlands venue a year ago, they were an insurgency provoking intrigue and attention and demonstrating plenty of momentum.Indeed that momentum was so significant that it was a major factor, perhaps the major factor, in accelerating the demise of Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister, because the potential prospect of a Reform government frightened the Labour Party to its core. Would Starmer, its then desperately unpopular leader, help or hinder their attempts to take on Farage? Hinder was the eventually overwhelming view within Labour, and so Starmer was a goner.But politics can change, and change quickly. With Starmer out and Burnham in, there is early evidence of some support for Labour picking up. No longer are Reform comfortably leading in all the opinion polls - in some they're not leading at all. Add to this a more confident and prominent Kemi Badenoch leading the Conservatives and the recent rise too of Restore Britain, the outfit set up by the former Reform MP Rupert Lowe. And the Scottish National Party and Plaid Cymru won and so beat them in the devolved elections in Scotland and Wales respectively. In other words, collectively Reform's opponents appear more energised and popular.Make no mistake, no party at a UK wide level is popular at the moment, but the scrap appears more evenly matched than it did.Into that mix, Reform's continued prominence has brought what prominence always brings: scrutiny. Nigel Farage is a candidate for prime minister; his senior team candidates for the great offices of state.When I interviewed Farage at Reform HQ yesterday, on the specifics of the £5m gift and the police investigation he maintained they've acted appropriately.But he offered an insight into how he perceives the hurricane of questions he faces."I think what you're seeing is the establishment - in a very coordinated way - fighting back," he claimed.I suggested he sounded like a conspiracy theorist, implying the whole world was out to get him.His answer was instructive: "When you read in the newspaper you're under investigation, and you don't even know a complaint's been made, you can see the degree of collusion that has gone on between interested parties. This will not stop. They will continually try and do this to us."Who's they? I pressed. He mentioned the House of Commons and House of Lords – full of his political opponents – but didn't name anyone or anything else."I'm talking about normal human behaviour. People who, people who hold positions of power, influence, and money don't want new kids on the block succeeding."Let's be clear – it is a big claim to allege collusion between institutions or organisations collectively seeking to undermine him and his party, and there is no evidence for it.But, crucially, you hear in his answer a sense of why he perceives that - that is what it feels like.The question, as Reform's conference gets under way, is how the party approaches the coming days and the coming months.Will Nigel Farage ditch the "aggrieved" tone he has been accused of adopting recently?

schema.headline: Chris Mason: Reform face headwinds as they gather for conference

title: Milford Haven boy, 16, who stabbed teacher in head sentenced to four years
description: Pupil who stabbed teacher in head given four-year detention orderImage caption, Teacher Vicki Williams told the court she feared she would die after t
body: Pupil who stabbed teacher in head given four-year detention orderImage caption, Teacher Vicki Williams told the court she feared she would die after the 16-year-old stabbed her at schoolByMeleri WilliamsBBC WalesReporting fromSwansea Crown CourtUpdated 4 hours agoA pupil who stabbed a teacher in the head with a kitchen knife after asking her to check his homework has been sentenced to four-and-a-half years in youth detention.The 16-year-old boy followed Vicki Williams into her empty classroom at Milford Haven Comprehensive School, Pembrokeshire, after asking for help with his work on 5 February.The teenager pulled a knife from his bag and lunged at her,  Swansea Crown Court previously heard, with Williams saying she feared she would die.After the trial in July, he was found not guilty of attempted murder but guilty of wounding with intent.On Thursday, Judge Thomas told the court there was a "significant degree of planning" and that "time stood still" for Williams.During the trial, Williams said the attack "came out of nowhere" after the boy - who cannot be named due to a court order - asked her for help with his work at the end of the school day.He closed the classroom door behind him and Williams noticed him looking through his bag as he asked her if his work "was correct". She said he suddenly pulled a large kitchen knife from the bag, and stabbed her in her head.Williams grabbed the knife, pushed the boy back with her legs, and screamed. She had injuries to her head, back and hands and said the boy looked at her with "pure hatred".Image source, CPSImage caption, The boy told the jury he had brought the knife to school as a "game" with his friendsDuring the sentencing hearing, the court heard Williams did not know if she would be able to return to work.She will start therapy for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) this week, and said in her victim personal statement that she felt "sadness, anger and guilt" after the incident."Sadness is the most predominant, I focus too much on what could have happened to me," she added."I'm in disbelief about what's happened."She said her daughter had "almost been left without a mum"."I'm scared because I don't know what I'm going to do going forward," she added."My fellow teachers and I don't deserve this because we work so hard."I didn't ask for this. Leaving teaching should have been my choice to make."She said she had returned to the school with a colleague during the summer holidays, and had realised how closely she had been "pinned" to the wall behind her desk.Image source, Pembrokeshire HeraldImage caption, Milford Haven Comprehensive School was locked down after the incident During the trial, a colleague who rushed to help described Williams's screams as "gut-wrenching".CCTV footage showed the teenager running away from the school after the attack.He was later detained at his grandmother's house after telling her that "something went" in his head.The boy told the jury he had brought the knife to school as a "game" with his friends, which involved bringing "random household objects" to see what they could "get away with".He said the incident was "an accident" and previously pleaded guilty to possessing a bladed article on school premises.During the hearing on Thursday, he stood in the dock in a blue shirt, with his family in the public gallery.Matthew Roberts, defending him, said he was of "clean character" and "well behaved" before the incident.He told the court his client had made "excellent progress" since being in youth detention.The boy is due to be released after half of the sentence period, but the court heard his release date could be changed depending on potential amendments to the early release scheme.Image caption, The council said there were a small number of pupils on site at the timeSentencing the boy to four-and-a-half years in a youth detention centre, Thomas said it was "pure luck" Williams had not been seriously injured or worse."I don't know why you attacked Mrs Williams with that knife, you never told anybody why you did it," the judge said."I think it may have been that in some way she had upset you, but I don't know for certain why."What I do know for certain is that you took a knife that day to school because you wanted to really hurt her with it."He added the boy knew he was "bigger and stronger" than Williams."It was pure luck that she didn't have far worse injuries, even fatal injuries," he said.The judge also referred to another school stabbing in south-west Wales, at Ysgol Dyffryn Aman, where a teenager stabbed two teachers and a pupil in April 2024."The court have to try and keep teachers safe from attacks," he said."This is the second case of a school pupil stabbing a teacher in a school in the last couple of years."I want anyone who is ever thinking of doing the same to know what will happen to them."Jonathan Pritchard, of the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), said the incident was a "shocking display of violence" towards a "teacher doing their job"."The teacher showed great courage in what must have been a terrifying incident," he said.

schema.headline: Milford Haven boy, 16, who stabbed teacher in head sentenced to four years

title: RuPaul's Drag Race UK welcomes the "Ru Generation"
description: They were raised on Drag Race UK - but can they snatch the crown?Image source, BBC/World of Wonder/Nick StrasburgImage caption, Mocha says Drag Race i
body: They were raised on Drag Race UK - but can they snatch the crown?Image source, BBC/World of Wonder/Nick StrasburgImage caption, Mocha says Drag Race inspired her to get into drag ByNaomi ClarkeBBC NewsbeatA new batch of queens from across the UK are set to battle it out in the hope of hearing RuPaul's magical words: "Condragulations, you're a winner, baby". The UK edition of Drag Race has been putting hopeful contestants through their paces for seven years - plenty of time for a new wave of talent raised on the hit reality show to emerge. Now "Generation Ru" are ready to compete for the crown and £25,000 cash prize.Series eight contestant Mocha, 26, tells BBC Newsbeat she considers herself part of this new cohort.  "My drag has always been inspired by Drag Race because that's why I started," the Essex-born queen says. "I think watching Drag Race made me realise that all of these things that I grew up wanting to do - like be a fashion designer, be a singer, like be a dancer, do makeup - it's actually all these things combined and I can be all of them at once." Image source, BBC/World of Wonder/Nick StrasburgImage caption, Flesh is fighting for the crown after her best friend Bones took the title last seasonMocha, who describes herself as a "fashion clown" and musical theatre lover, says it has taken her nearly a decade to get to this stage but feels it is the "right time".And while watching the show has influenced her style and given her a something to work towards, she says the process isn't for those who just want to get on TV."Drag is hard and you've got to love it, you've got to have a passion for it," she says. "Drag Race is the extra-special prize you get at the end, but it's not the main goal in that way." London-based queen and fellow contestant Flesh agrees she is "100% Generation Ru"."I found drag through queens who had featured in the American franchise," the 26-year-old says. "And from the first season of the UK franchise I was hooked, I was a fan."It has always really been my blueprint.“She has also developed her "supermodel of Soho" style alongside her best friend Bones, the reigning Drag Race UK Superstar.Flesh says she was "so happy" for her drag sister when she won, but it also made her "terrified" to compete this year as she focused on proving herself. Image source, BBC/World of Wonder/Nick StrasburgImage caption, Naya Thorn says the expense of preparing for the show almost led her to drop-outAlmost 100 queens have lip-synced their way through Drag Race UK's challenges, but there are fans who worry whether the British scene can support more series of the annual show.Series eight's youngest contestant, Naya Thorn, who was 23 when she was chosen for the show, feels there are new queens cropping up all over the UK.But she admits the show would benefit if more "seasoned and colourful characters" from across the scene got involved.However, she says, cost-of-living pressures are putting a strain on queens trying to make it.Naya, from Dudley, West Midlands, says the expense of preparing for the show almost led her to drop-out, and she wouldn't have been TV-ready without her support network at home."It really upsets me that there's a lot of people that would do well on the show and should have that platform that feel like they can't go on because of how expensive it seems to be getting," she says. "But I am here to prove to everyone, you don't need that much money." Image source, BC/World of Wonder/Nick StrasburgImage caption, Series eight contestant Paris Baby feels the new season will usher in a "drag renaissance"Flesh, who has been running a drag show for the past five years, says she has also seen turnout at live performances drop, and feels soaring costs have likely impacted that. She thinks the TV show still appeals as it provides "the joy and the power of drag from the comfort of your own home", but says this comes at a price to performers."Expectations remain at a Drag Race level and our income and opportunities in the real world do not reflect that," she says. The Soho-based queen also says social media has become a "double-edged sword".Although it's vital to advertise live shows, "the more you show... the less inclined people are to go", she says.Flesh adds: "If the public aren't willing to support drag outside of the Drag Race vehicle" then "we won't be able to sustain Drag Race".The queens this year will be hoping to spark more interest into the show and drag, including Paris Baby, who describes herself as "UK's British Bajan Barbie".She has been hailing the new series as the "drag renaissance" as she feels it was a "really strong" year and hopes it will be "very well received" internationally."Hopefully we can bring a little 'je ne sais quoi' and reignite the interest in drag," she says.RuPaul's Drag Race UK series eight launches at 22:00 BST on BBC Three and is available to watch on BBC iPlayer.Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.

schema.headline: RuPaul's Drag Race UK welcomes the "Ru Generation"

title: Schools to close early for A66 crash funeral
description: Cleveland Police said they were expecting the event to cause traffic disruption and delays, adding it had plans in place to ensure public safety.South
body: Cleveland Police said they were expecting the event to cause traffic disruption and delays, adding it had plans in place to ensure public safety.South Bank Primary School and Outwood Academy Normanby are among the four schools which have confirmed they will close at lunchtime because of concerns about the impact of the funeral on pupils, staff and families.Archway Academy in Teesville has confirmed it will close at 11:45 BST and St Margaret Clitherow's Catholic Primary School in South Bank at 12:15.South Bank Primary School said it was closing early "to ensure the safety and wellbeing of our pupils".Head teacher Tammy Cooper said large numbers of people were expected in the area for the funeral at St John's Church on Normanby Road.The school also said some pupils might feel "upset or anxious" about the funeral and that its pastoral team would be available to provide support.In a letter to parents, Mark Robinson, principal of Outwood Academy Normanby, said the school would also close early following discussions between local headteachers and the council.Redcar and Cleveland Council said the Mackenzie Thorpe Centre will be closed all day and some SEND children who live in the South Bank area and attend other schools may be collected earlier in the day.Supt John Wrintmore from Cleveland Police said there was potential for traffic disruption and delays from 15:00 to 17:00 on Friday."This will affect areas of South Bank, Normanby Road through Teesville, Ormesby and Marton, and Acklam Road," he said."We are working closely with highways departments from the local authority, who are leading on the traffic management for this event, in order to minimise disruption."As with any significant gathering, we have plans in place to ensure public safety and security, which is line with our usual process."A spokesperson for Redcar & Cleveland Borough Council said: "A number of schools in the South Bank area will close earlier than usual on Friday afternoon due to anticipated traffic congestion and transport disruption associated with a local funeral taking place in the area."The decision was made after careful consideration of the potential impact on home-to-school transport and the departure of pupils, staff and families at the end of the school day."Schools have worked with the Local Authority and transport providers to consider arrangements for pupils, including those who travel to and from specialist educational settings."We recognise that early closure may cause inconvenience for some parents and carers, and we thank them for their understanding and cooperation."The decision comes after a vigil, for one of the young men who died, last week was followed by disorder in Haswell, County Durham, where a number of cars were set on fire.The incident prompted criticism from MPs and police.The Volkswagen Passat involved in the collision was being pursued by police until 10 seconds before the crash, according to the police watchdog.The Independent Office for Police Conduct said the Passat was believed to be using cloned registration plates.A total of 27 people have been arrested as part of a wider police operation against organised crime, following the crash.Follow BBC Tees on X,, external Facebook, external, Nextdoor and Instagram, external.

schema.headline: Schools to close early for A66 crash funeral

title: USS Abraham Lincoln: US sailors unwind in Thailand by shopping and bar-hopping
description: US sailors go shopping before hitting the bars in Thailand after 250-day voyageFigure caption, Watch: Why US troops have a history in this raucous Tha
body: US sailors go shopping before hitting the bars in Thailand after 250-day voyageFigure caption, Watch: Why US troops have a history in this raucous Thai cityByJonathan Head and Nongnapat PatchamReporting fromPattaya, ThailandUpdated 4 hours agoFar from hitting the bars and fleshpots of the Thai beach resort of Pattaya, in their first hours onshore most of the nearly 5,000 sailors from the USS Abraham Lincoln seemed determined to go shopping.At the Hard Rock Hotel – one of two beachside hotels where they were able to stay off the ship – they hung around clutching their recent purchases. But perhaps, after a record 250 days confined inside a grey steel warship, the normality of a trip to the mall might have been just what they needed. With their military haircuts, moustaches and navy t-shirts, they stood out against the usual Pattaya crowd in flip-flops and beachwear.Image source, ReutersImage caption, US sailors arrived in Thailand on WednesdayNight, though, is when this resort city comes into its own, putting on a riotous spectacle of neon, noise and naughty bars. Pattaya's tourism industry has been hit by conflict in the Middle East, where the USS Abraham Lincoln was last operating, with many of the tourists the city depends on choosing to stay at home.Local establishments have been hoping American sailors, arriving with nine months of unspent salary while at sea, will provide a much-needed boost. On Wednesday night, the city's most famous promenade, Walking Street, was very much open to them, with a huge, illuminated sign at its entrance welcoming the crew of the US carrier. They have, however, been reminded the sex industry is off-limits, as prostitution is technically illegal in Thailand. But alcohol was flowing. By midnight some of the younger sailors were so inebriated they had to prop each other up. Others edged nervously into the red-lit caverns of the go-go bars, with their gyrating and barely-clothed pole dancers.Image caption, Bar owner Kanta Saenkla said she'd seen fewer sailors coming to her establishment compared to the past Conversation over the pounding music was challenging. One older crew member told us they really needed the break. "The news says we've been at sea for nine months. To be honest I've lost track of time," he said. "It got boring. It's never big enough on board. It's big but it still feels like a boat, especially when you're sharing it with thousands of people." How long would it take them to get home to California? "Too long," he said.Restaurant owner Kosol Homkhunthod said the American sailors had "created a buzz" in town and among his staff - business had been "really slow" lately.And a passing tourist described seeing "tonnes of people sitting on the beach", with soldiers in good spirits. "It's not like that every day."But bar owner Kanta Saenkla complained many of the sailors appeared to simply be roaming around rather than enjoying the local bars."They haven't really come in for drinks or anything," she said. "Mostly they just walk around. They're not spending money like they did in previous years."Image caption, Pattaya is renowned for its racy and neon-lit nightlifeOut partying or not, Pattaya is a welcome respite for the crew.Shakeira Fairfax, mother of 25-year-old sailor Jada Fairfax, told Reuters there had been moments over the past few months when "morale was low". She described the period after hostilities broke out in the Middle East as an "uncertain" and "scary" time."I just can't wait to see her smile. I can't wait to hear 'mum', I know that's the first thing she's gonna say," Fairfax added.The crew have been well-drilled not to talk about conditions on board the USS Abraham Lincoln during its long combat deployment in the operation against Iran, which have been the subject of criticism back in the US. Some sailors were wary of making any conversation at all. Others referred journalists' questions to their media teams. Visible everywhere in Pattaya were the men wearing t-shirts emblazoned with the letters SLG, or Shore Liaison Group. It is their job to maintain discipline on land, to watch out for the crew members, some of whom are very young and inexperienced, and to co-ordinate with the local authorities during port calls.US Naval Attache Kristopher Robinson did not answer questions from the BBC about activities that soldiers were banned from doing while in Pattaya, saying that "we're trying to give the sailors as much opportunity for rest as they can".US personnel, he added, would "conduct themselves in accordance with US law, US naval regulations, and the laws of Thailand".Image source, ReutersImage caption, The nuclear-powered aircraft carrier has spent nine months at seaThe decision by the USS Abraham Lincoln to stop in Pattaya makes a lot of sense. Port calls by the US Navy in Thailand, a long-standing treaty ally, are routine with well-established protocols. It is also on the ship's route from the Gulf to California, giving the crew a chance to let off steam, and enjoy a break from the demands of life on board a warship.If their stop in Thailand does the trick, any frustration they may feel over their unexpectedly long and tough mission may have dissipated by the time they get home.

schema.headline: USS Abraham Lincoln: US sailors unwind in Thailand by shopping and bar-hopping

title: El Niño 'supersized' as countries race to prepare for extreme weather, UN warns
description: Image source, Luis Tato/AFP/Getty ImagesImage caption, Countries in East Africa, like Kenya, experienced intense rainfall during the last El Niño even
body: Image source, Luis Tato/AFP/Getty ImagesImage caption, Countries in East Africa, like Kenya, experienced intense rainfall during the last El Niño eventByEsme Stallardsenior climate and science reporterMark Poynting and Becky DaleBBC Verify and Yvette Tan, Tiffanie Turnbull and Nikita YadavThe world has entered a "danger zone of extreme weather" as the impacts of El Niño start to be felt globally, UN head António Guterres has warned.The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) has released the latest data on the natural weather phenomenon showing it could be the strongest for more than 70 years and last until at least February 2027.El Niño changes weather patterns around the world, pushing some regions into drought whilst others experience stronger typhoons and flooding.Forecasters also say El Niño will boost temperatures in some places, coming on top of rising heat globally from human-induced climate change."El Niño is being supersized before our eyes. The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up," Guterres said.The BBC spoke with governments and scientists about the measures being taken globally to reduce the risk of deaths, displacement and environmental damage. Early warning systems have been strengthened and deployment of pre-emptive medical assistance, but the strength of this particular event has raised serious concerns particularly for vulnerable groups.The WMO - a UN agency -  said it has undertaken a "major mobilisation" to try to circulate its forecasts of potential extreme weather events, linked to El Niño, to as many communities as possible.WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo warned: "El Niño has the potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world."El Niño is a natural weather phenomenon that develops in the Pacific Ocean and is linked to a change in wind patterns. It allows warm water to spread eastwards and releases heat into the atmosphere.Sea temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific have risen sharply in recent months - a clear sign of a strengthening El Niño.In the Pacific's key monitoring region, surface temperatures have been well over 2C above average in recent weeks, putting it on track to be declared a "very strong" event.But it is expected to surpass even that marker. Monthly sea surface temperatures could get close to 4C above average, forecasts suggest.This would make it the strongest El Niño since at least 1950, by potentially a large margin.Temperatures are even more exceptional below the surface of the Pacific - in places more than 8C above average.Above-normal sea temperatures are also expected in other parts of the world including the Indian Ocean, tropical Atlantic and around parts of the Australian coast.With its rich marine life, changes in ocean heat are of particular concern to Australia.It has been plagued by marine heatwaves in recent years - driven by climate change - leading to widespread coral bleaching and algae blooms, causing "unprecedented damage". El Niño is a natural phenomenon, but it tends to bring the kind of extreme heat which also drives those disasters, Dr Alistair Hobday, chief researcher at Australia's science agency, told the BBC.This year, marine heatwave forecasts indicate the Great Barrier Reef will be spared the worst of the conditions, giving coral there more time to recover."[But] Southern Australia is getting slammed. It had an algal bloom last year, it's got bird flu now, and it looks like marine heatwaves will be stronger there this summer," said Hobday.Last time a marine heatwave hit South Australia and Tasmania, there were starving penguins, fish kills, suffocating algae outbreaks, and jellyfish invasions.Australia has recently introduced early warning systems for marine crises - this gives time for financial relief for fisheries to be established, relocation of crucial species and increased coral monitoring.But this event is shaping up to be unprecedented - and Hobday admits he is quite worried.Reduced rainfall brings drought and trade disruptionWhile the impacts on global weather are likely to be felt well into 2027, the WMO expects significant changes in rainfall patterns over the next few months.Drier-than-usual conditions are forecast across large areas of South East Asia, Central America and northern parts of South America, increasing the risk of droughts and wildfires.On Thursday, the number of vessels passing through the Panama Canal will be reduced by more than 10% in anticipation of lower rainfall.About 14,000 ships per year use the artificial waterway - as well as being a crucial route for global trade, it is also a key source of income for Panama, bringing in about $3bn (£2.2bn) a year.Indonesia is racing to contain wildfires that have burned more than 107,000 hectares of land nationwide this dry season. Like some other parts of South East Asia, it is facing a longer season this year.A resident in Central Kalimantan told BBC News Indonesia he had been experiencing wildfires "for more than a month"."The smoke has become quite thick. When we step outside, our eyes start to sting. The smell of the smoke is also quite strong," said Darwin Romy.Authorities have said they are deploying cloud-seeding aircraft to trigger rains to extinguish these fires, and its government has promised resources to contain the fire and arrested dozens over allegations of using it to clear land.Image source, Monirul Bhuiyan/AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Countries in Southern Africa, like Botswana, experienced severe drought during the last El Niño eventStronger typhoons and landslide riskThousands of miles away, China is expecting seven typhoons to make landfall in this year alone – something the country's experts have said is linked to the effects of a super El Niño.In July alone, China experienced three typhoons - Bavi, Noul and Maysak - which left dozens dead.And in August, more than a million people were forced to evacuate their homes as Typhoon Dolphin hit – bringing heavy rains and strong winds.Similarly, wetter-than-average weather is expected in parts of eastern Africa, southern Brazil and the southern US, raising the chances of flooding."We are already seeing disruption and devastation from droughts and floods and we expect these impacts to increase as El Niño intensifies," said Prof Celeste Saulo, secretary general of the WMO.This is all happening on top of long-term human-caused warming, making the impacts potentially more intense. Some scientists believe climate change could even be making El Niño events stronger, but this is not yet certain.Celeste Saulo, WMO: Extreme weather is the new normalAvailable now on BBC SoundsPeru is particularly vulnerable to El Niño, as its coastline borders the eastern Pacific.Parts of the country, along with Ecuador and parts of Brazil, have previously experienced increased rainfall, resulting in flash flooding and landslides, particularly in urban centres where the water is less able to drain away.Miguel Aréstegui, climate resilience lead at Practical Action, which helps countries prepare for extreme weather, said "we are significantly concerned, but that concern needs to translate into preparedness rather than alarm."He said Practical Action had been working with partners over recent years to make sure the public had better access to early warning systems, including sharing information on river levels, flood risks and weather forecasts.At the end of last month, the US announced it was deploying the vessel USNS Comfort to the Peruvian coast to provide additional medical assistance and technical equipment for when El Niño reaches its peak.However, Aréstegui said El Niño "does not arrive in a vacuum". There are bigger, structural issues that make these events worse and which take much longer to resolve such as "housing in exposed areas, fragile water and sanitation systems, and a weak healthcare system", he said.Get in touchWhat questions or concerns do you have about El Niño?

schema.headline: El Niño 'supersized' as countries race to prepare for extreme weather, UN warns

title: Mike Dean: Ex-referee says he played in-match games 'for a laugh'
description: Former Premier League referee Mike Dean says he used to set himself mini-challenges during matches "as a laugh".Appearing on Jamie Vardy's podcast, De
body: Former Premier League referee Mike Dean says he used to set himself mini-challenges during matches "as a laugh".Appearing on Jamie Vardy's podcast, Dean said he would see how long he could go without blowing his whistle, or stay inside the centre circle."We used to say, 'we'll kick off now. Right, see how long we can go without blowing a whistle'," he added."I've done that a few times in the Premier League, before VAR obviously - went 20, 25 minutes without blowing a whistle."I used to do another thing. I used to stand in the centre circle - see how long I could stay in the centre circle before I had to leave."That was just me joking about. I got about 15 minutes once."Mark Halsey, who refereed in the Premier League between 1999 and 2013, told BBC Sport that Dean's comments damaged the reputation of all referees.BBC Sport understands that refereeing figures consider Dean's claims to be unfounded, which would be historical and go back to the pre-video assistant referee era before 2019, when Pro Ref was under different leadership.It is not the first time he has courted controversy for his media statements.When acting as the video assistant referee (VAR) for Chelsea's 2-2 draw with Tottenham in August 2022, Dean failed to send the referee to the monitor for a red card for Cristian Romero.The Spurs defender should have been penalised for pulling Marc Cucurella's hair.After retiring, Dean said in an interview he did not intervene because he wanted to save referee Anthony Taylor from extra "grief"."I didn't want to send him up because he is a mate as well as a referee," he revealed.Dean enjoyed a 28-year career as a professional official, stepping down from on-field officiating in 2022 and retiring after spending the 2022-23 season as a full-time VAR.The 58-year-old began officiating in 1985 and progressed from refereeing in the Football League 10 years later, and then to Premier League in 2000.Dean refereed the 2008 FA Cup final and 2011 League Cup final at Wembley.Halsey also doubted Dean's story was true, but he had questions to answer if so. "It's caused so much controversy, and in all my years as a professional referee I have never heard of these these games, never," said Halsey."If Mike has played these games, then he's done that of his own accord. "And if he has, then I think we need to know what games he's done them in, and how many games he's done them in. It brings into question the integrity of every official now."Halsey added he had spoken to other officials today who said "they've not heard of it either", as he questioned the validity of Dean's claims."It's just impossible to go five minutes, let alone 20 minutes, without blowing your whistle to giving a free-kick," he said.When Dean said in 2023 that he had helped out "a mate" in the Chelsea-Tottenham game from a year earlier, it caused real damage to the reputation of referees.Officials have to deal with baseless allegations of corruption and favouritism as it is, so giving any kind of credence to a lack of professionalism by a referee is a problem.As one serving referee told me at the time, it was as though Dean had "thrown them all under a bus". It tars everyone with the same brush, regardless of the facts.Dean's revelations this week are not quite so explosive, and it is difficult to know whether, if true, they could have an impact on a game.Of course, if Dean refused to blow his whistle to give a penalty because he was playing one of these games, that is a different matter.But without Dean giving any specific examples, it could equally be the case that he was trying to make himself come across as 'one of the boys' when chatting with ex-players. After making the claim, comedian and podcast co-host Josh James jokingly said to Dean: "Easy money."  Refereeing bosses consider Dean to be of the old school, a different era when the organisation may not have been quite so professional and progressive.But even though it is more than four years since Dean stepped out onto a football pitch he remains as well-known as most current referees.And when he says something controversial, it is going to get traction.

schema.headline: Mike Dean: Ex-referee says he played in-match games 'for a laugh'

title: Benhard Janse van Rensburg knew nothing of potential South Africa call-up
description: Centre Benhard Janse van Rensburg has admitted that he "probably would have loved to" play for his native South Africa, but denied Rassie Erasmus' cla
body: Centre Benhard Janse van Rensburg has admitted that he "probably would have loved to" play for his native South Africa, but denied Rassie Erasmus' claim he was in talks over a Springboks call-up before making his England debut.Janse van Rensburg, who represented South Africa's under-20 side, became eligible for England this summer after living in the country for five years and scored on his Test bow against Fiji in Liverpool in July.The previous week South Africa head coach Erasmus had claimed Van Rensburg had been "very keen" in talks with Springboks officials, but ultimately wasn't selected."I only heard about it because my dad told me Rassie said it," Janse van Rensburg told Rugby Union Weekly."I would have probably loved to, but really every team I play for, I want to do my best and whatever comes after that, comes after that."When Rassie said he wanted to pick me, I was in the dark."I hadn't heard anything from them. Whatever he said, whether that was true or not, I didn't know about it."The selection of the 29-year-old for England ahead of talents brought through the domestic system has attracted criticism.Danny Care, who won 101 caps in his England career, said Janse van Rensburg's selection "doesn't sit right",  while former centres Jeremy Guscott, external and Mike Tindall , externalalso questioned the call.Janse van Rensburg has tried to avoid the commentary around his promotion into the England team, but says he can see its critics' perspective."It is understandable that that there's going to be some people that don't like it and some people that do like it," he added."People probably still have their thoughts and how they feel about it."For me, I probably can't prove them wrong. I just want to do my best for whichever team I play for."It's an honour and a privilege to go to that next level of playing rugby."Janse van Rensburg crossed for a try three minutes after coming on for Henry Slade in the 73-8 win over Fiji, before also appearing off the bench in the 31-24 win in Argentina the following weekend.He says his integration has been eased by having previously played the Call of Duty video game against some of the squad, with a Leicester group including Jack van Poortvliet, George Martin and Freddie Steward joining him online.While on tour this summer, he has been successful in more analogue pursuits."I think I made about 300-odd pounds on tour, just by winning all the cards," he said"At Bristol we play, but not for money, so I've just gotten good at it. And then, as soon as it was for money, I just pocketed."All of the boys have just made me feel like I'm playing a normal game for my local club. They made me feel so welcome and it is so easy for me to not have any nerves and just go and enjoy it."

schema.headline: Benhard Janse van Rensburg knew nothing of potential South Africa call-up

title: Italian Grand Prix: Lewis Hamilton says upgraded Ferrari engine 'step forward but not whole amount we need'
description: Hamilton and team-mate Charles Leclerc have both won one race this season, with the Briton 59 points behind championship leader Kimi Antonelli of Merc
body: Hamilton and team-mate Charles Leclerc have both won one race this season, with the Briton 59 points behind championship leader Kimi Antonelli of Mercedes."To win this weekend, the whole collective has to come together. Everything has to flow from the beginning," said Hamilton."There is a first ahead of me, in the sense of if I was to win I go into new territory winning for the first time in Ferrari at Monza. It would be phenomenal. "The pressure's high. You want to do it for the team. Many of them will come to this race. The tifosi come out in huge numbers with a passion that's unmatched. "And my mum's here. I don't think she's been to Monza, and certainly not (while I was) with Ferrari. I wanted her to experience this and bring any lucky dust she can bring."Ferrari's hopes of a home victory are boosted by the fact that Italian Antonelli will have a grid penalty for exceeding his permitted number of engine parts and is likely to start at the back.Hamilton said: "There is big gap between the top teams and the rest. Kimi will start from the back but with the power he has, and the performance he has, he should slide through that pack pretty easy and it's probably why they chose this race to do that."So achieving eighth or sixth should be relatively easy. We have to focus on maximising our weekend and try and take the energy from the tifosi to hopefully push us to the front."Antonelli's grid penalty was inevitable at some point after reliability problems earlier in the year meant they would need to exceed his allowance of four engines for the season.They chose this weekend because they calculated it was the most optimal race to do it, both in terms of the effect of a new engine on a track dominated by straights, and managing their engine pool through the rest of the year.Team-mate George Russell will also have an engine penalty, most likely in Azerbaijan in two races' time.Antonelli said: "I am very much looking forward to this weekend despite starting from the back. I will be able to enjoy it more than I did previously and hopefully we will still be able to have a good race."In some ways it helps to release pressure, although I would very much rather fight for pole and start at the front."It makes me a bit more relaxed going into the weekend. I think this track can be very good for us but we have to take into account that McLaren, Ferrari, even Red Bull can be good this weekend."There are other tracks where it is possible to overtake but this one is very energy starved and there are a lot of places where you can race differently and it gives us the best chance to climb through the field."Antonelli referred to energy starvation because the hybrid engines will be without their battery power for a higher percentage of the lap in Monza than at most races this year, because of the long straights and the lack of opportunity for recovery.Drivers are expecting a difficult and frustrating weekend, and for slipstreaming, which saves energy by reducing drag, to become a major feature in qualifying and the grand prix.Antonelli said he expected speed would flat-line on the straights but not drop significantly, and that the situation would be "better than many expected".Hamilton arrived at Monza for media day on Thursday in his new Ferrari F40, an iconic 1980s supercar, which he described as "a dream car of mine".He explained why the particular model he chose was so important to him, and a surprise resonance he discovered to his race number, which is 44.The seven-time champion said: "I have been looking for one for a while. I wanted one with low mileage and a story behind it. Lots have come up at auction but not particularly special. Or the paint's been redone. I wanted to find the most authentic one."I found this one that a guy bought it and drove it 69km from Maranello to his home and parked it and never drove it again."Then the decision is, 'Do you keep it as an art piece, all dusty, or clean it up?' That took a while to decide."I might be wrong but none of the Ferrari drivers in history have ever arrived in the coolest car in history."When they were taking the car apart... it has 44 stamped on the engine. I couldn't believe it. So it feels very much fate."He chose to drive it to the track, he said, "because I thought it was an opportunity to highlight the history of Ferrari in their own country and their race."

schema.headline: Italian Grand Prix: Lewis Hamilton says upgraded Ferrari engine 'step forward but not whole amount we need'

title: Chicken Shop Date to end as host says 'time to move on'
description: "To me the show is my very own rom-com and I have loved creating so many stories for you to watch," she wrote."I am so grateful to everyone who has fo
body: "To me the show is my very own rom-com and I have loved creating so many stories for you to watch," she wrote."I am so grateful to everyone who has followed me on this journey and found some joy in these episodes."I never thought I'd stop Chicken Shop Date, I thought maybe it would be a part of me forever, and in some way it always will, but I feel like it's now time to move on from this adventure and on to a new one."Dimoldenberg insisted just months ago she had no plans to end Chicken Shop Date, and said she planned to carry on until she met her "one true love".Her most recent interviewees have included music heavyweight Paul McCartney, Swedish pop star  Zara Larsson and US television host Conan O'Brien. The presenter has long said her dream guest, external would be Drake and fans will be speculating if she's managed to bag the Canadian rapper for one of her final episodes.And thousands of supportive comments have been left under the announcement post. Radio 1 presenter and podcaster Jamie Laing wrote: "The G.O.A.T."Author and broadcaster Elizabeth Day wrote: "Knowing when to stop - and leaving on such a high, after shaping the culture - is the quintessential power move."Rapper Tinie Tempah commented: "Smashed it!"Dimoldenberg previously told the BBC how Chicken Shop Date had grown out of a series of interviews with grime artists she conducted as a teenager for culture magazine The Cut."I started Chicken Shop Date as part of a youth club, and we made a magazine, and everything I learned there, the connections I made, the mentoring I got, set me up for the career that I have today," she said.

title: Fly brain wiring map may hold clues for autism and schizophrenia
description: Scientists have managed to compare the fine detail of the brains of male and female flies for the first time, identifying differences they say explain
body: Scientists have managed to compare the fine detail of the brains of male and female flies for the first time, identifying differences they say explain male aggression, courtship and their singing of love songs.The scientists in Cambridge mapped all 124 million connections of nerve cells in a male fly's brain, having done the same for a female fly two years ago.The team are clear that the research won't explain differences between men and women because our behaviour is far more complex.But the research could help scientists better understand human behaviour and conditions in which genetic differences affect brain wiring, such as autism and schizophrenia.Prof Gregory Jefferis, of the Medical Research Council's Laboratory of Molecular Biology and University of Cambridge, who co-led the research, told BBC News that the breakthrough was "a really important new avenue in neuroscience", likening it to the invention of a powerful new telescope in increasing our understanding of the Universe."We have this amazing stuff in our heads that lets us do incredible things such as playing a sonata or solving a scientific problem. And this development could help our understanding of how those  systems work".The small differences they discovered can lead to big changes in behaviour.In courtship, for example, the male tracks the female as she moves. The researchers have identified the brain circuits associated with that trait and found key differences in the wiring. The males have extra bits that should enhance his visual tracking.There is an even bigger difference in the circuits associated with aggression. Males fight more often and so there is much more wiring associated with that behaviour than in females.And then, there is the love song circuit.Males woo females by producing a sound. They have wiring unique only to them to producee the sound. According to Dr Philipp Schlegel, co-author of the study, the circuit has to be just right, otherwise the consequneces for the poor male could be dire."The courtship also includes singing to the female," he told me. "The sound is produced by vibrating the wings to produce a very specific song."If the female likes it, she will allow him to approach, and if she doesn't, and she's not receptive at a time, she'll basically reject him, which could be a kick to the face".These three differences between male and female wiring in flies are driven by two key genes. Researchers have known about the genes for years, and how they're linked to each of these behaviours. What they've never been able to see is the bit in the middle. Now, for the first time, they can see the actual wiring those genes produce.The primary aim of the research was not to discover the differences between male and female flies, and certainly not to find neurological explanations for certain alleged behavioural differences between men and women. Comparing two brains that have some slight wiring differences associated with known big behavioural differences enables scientists to clearly see the principles that underlie the changes to brain wiring for all behaviour, according to Beckett."You just have one independent variable, the sex, and then you can see what's different. This is a scientist's dream".These differences take scientists a big step forward in understanding one of the biggest questions in biology - how genes influence behaviour. Scientists have known for decades that they do, but have had little idea of exactly how they exert their influence. The answer, according to Dr Jefferis, is in how the genes shape the brain's wiring and how that wiring influences behaviour."The fly brain comparison gives us a really good handle on this," he told BBC News."There are patterns of behaviour in humans that seem to have a strong genetic, basis. So, for example, there are many gene varients now related to schizophrenia and autism spectrum disorders that we don't really understand".
